analysis.one_liner: Restores the federal estate tax on the largest inheritances, with rates up to 55% and new limits on avoidance tricks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was referred there the day it was introduced in June 2010 and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2010 the federal estate tax had temporarily fallen to zero because of a scheduled expiration in the 2001 tax law. This bill would have brought the tax back for people dying after 2009: estates above about $3.5 million would be taxed, with rates rising from 39% to 55% on amounts over $50 million and an extra 10% surcharge on estates over $500 million. It also would have tightened rules wealthy families use to shrink taxable estates — like discounting the value of family-business stakes and very short-term trusts — while giving extra protection to family farms and land donated for conservation. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the general public through federal revenue, since the tax falls only on the largest estates — those above roughly $3.5 million per person — and the money goes to the treasury rather than to any group of taxpayers. Family farms and ranches would get extra protection through a larger special valuation reduction, and landowners donating conservation easements would get a bigger estate-tax break. Heirs would also get clearer, standardized valuation paperwork for inherited property.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General public; family farms and conservation donors

how_it_helps.text: It restores the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes for people dying after 2009, reversing the 2001 law's temporary repeal that left 2010 estates untaxed.
It raises revenue progressively: a 39% bracket starts only above $3.5 million, rates climb to 55% on amounts over $50 million, and a 10% surtax applies to the portion of estates over $500 million.

It closes avoidance techniques used by the wealthy, including valuation discounts for minority interests in family entities, assets parked in entities to shrink taxable values, and very short grantor retained annuity trusts.

It quadruples the special valuation reduction for farmland to $3 million and raises the estate-tax exclusion for donated conservation easements to $2 million, easing the burden on family farms and land conservation.

analysis.who_pays: Estates above the new thresholds — roughly, couples' estates over about $7 million and single estates over $3.5 million — would pay the tax, with the highest rates hitting estates over $50 million and a surtax over $500 million. Wealthy families who use valuation discounts, entity parking, or short grantor retained annuity trusts to shrink taxable estates would lose those techniques, and executors would face new reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Estates over ~$3.5 million; wealthy families using trusts

drawbacks.text: The bill raises rates sharply on large estates — 55% above $50 million plus a 10% surtax above $500 million — and critics of estate taxes argue this taxes wealth that was already taxed when it was earned, and can push wealthy families toward avoidance planning.

The new basis-reporting rules would require executors and gift-givers to file valuation statements for inherited and gifted property, adding paperwork for estates and heirs, and the limits on valuation discounts and shorter GRAT terms would reduce planning tools some family-business owners rely on.

While the bill increases farmland valuation relief and conservation easement exclusions, family businesses and farms that exceed the thresholds would still face estate tax bills that opponents say can force asset sales.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a tax falls almost entirely on the largest estates, with the money available for public priorities everyone shares, and the bill pairs the higher rates with extra protection for family farms and conservation donors — a good-faith answer to the most common objection. The costs are real but narrow: heavier paperwork for executors and heirs, tighter limits on estate-planning maneuvers, and higher bills for very wealthy families, which critics say can encourage avoidance and double-tax savings already taxed during life. The bill never advanced far enough for a full public weighing against a competing design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on June 24, 2010, joined by Senators Whitehouse, Harkin, Brown of Ohio, and Franken.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
During 2010 the estate tax stood at zero under the scheduled repeal, so the question of how to reinstate it was live; this bill was one proposal, and it never became the vehicle for the answer.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest estates and their heirs came out ahead: the estate tax stayed at zero for 2010 deaths, and the eventual December 2010 law set a far lower rate with a much larger exemption than this bill proposed. Anyone counting on estate-tax revenue for public priorities lost.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the estate tax with progressive rates and anti-avoidance rules.

for.name: 4 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Whitehouse, Harkin, Brown of Ohio, Franken)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no additional senators signed on and no committee or floor action followed.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: In the December 2010 tax-cut negotiations, agreed to a much smaller estate tax — a 35% rate with a $5 million exemption — rather than the higher rates and lower exemption in bills like this one, settling the issue without this bill ever coming to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all five sponsors were Democratic-caucus members (Sanders plus four Democrats), so support on record was entirely from one side of the aisle, but the opposition never had to show itself in a roll call.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and their heirs (estates over roughly $3.5 million)
industries.note: The bill reinstates and raises the estate tax these families had escaped in 2010 and closes the valuation discounts, entity-parking, and short-GRAT techniques used to shrink taxable estates. Because the bill died, they kept the lower-tax landscape instead.

The bill quadruples the special farmland valuation reduction to $3 million, letting more farm estates qualify for below-market valuation and reducing the risk that heirs sell land to pay the tax. The bill's death left this relief unenacted.

industries.industry: Land conservation donors and land trusts
industries.note: It raises the estate-tax exclusion for donated conservation easements to $2 million and increases the qualifying percentage, making it easier for landowners' estates to preserve land. This relief also died with the bill.

industries.industry: Estate-planning professionals and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Reinstating the tax sustains demand for estate planning, but the bill's limits on minority discounts, nonbusiness-asset parking, and short GRATs would curb the most lucrative avoidance structuring. Its death preserved the status quo planning market.
